shipped.kurz: Attila's court and the road to Gaul, 440–450
shipped.warum: Priscus' embassy to Attila in 448–449 in Bury's English: the wooden palace, a Greek who preferred the Huns and Priscus' answer, Attila judging at his door, the banquet and the wooden cup. Jordanes' portrait in Latin with a working translation: the murdered brother Bleda, 'a man born into the world to shake the nations', the sword of Mars. And three reasons for the war of 451 that do not exclude each other: Gaiseric's gifts, a war 'only against the Goths' (Jordanes and Prosper), and Honoria, the emperor's sister, claimed as a wife (the Gallic chronicle of 452).

How a coalition of old enemies came together. The wars of the 430s, when Aetius' general Litorius led Hunnic horsemen against the Goths and was taken at Toulouse (Jordanes, and Sidonius' panegyric on Avitus); Valentinian's embassy to Theoderic and the answer 'you have made Attila our enemy too'; the list of allies in Jordanes, copied from Prosper; a continuation of Prosper on the Franks 'who had no kings'; Sidonius' catalogue of Attila's peoples and Aetius begging Avitus to bring the Goths; Aetius commending himself to Saint Peter; and Sangiban the Alan, suspected of treason and watched in the middle of the line.

What the war meant city by city, as the churches remembered it. Gregory of Tours on Aravatius, told in Rome that the Huns could not be stopped, and on Metz burned on Easter eve; Orléans told three ways: by Gregory (relieved before the walls fell), by the Life of Anianus (the Huns already inside and drawing lots for the citizens), and by Sidonius, who promised a history of the siege and never wrote it and called Aetius 'the liberator of the Loire'; Lupus of Troyes taken by Attila to the Rhine; Genovefa nearly stoned by the Parisians as a false prophet. And beside the Lives, their editor Bruno Krusch's verdicts of 1896: late, dependent, 'invented from beginning to end'.

Jordanes' account section by section in Mommsen's Latin with a new English translation: the field 'also called Mauriacan', the soothsayers, the lines and the fight for the hill, Attila's speech, 'bellum atrox multiplex immane pertinax', the brook of blood, Theoderic's death told two ways, the wagon fort and the pyre of saddles, Aetius' advice to Thorismud and 165,000 dead. Against it, every chronicle that mentions the battle: Prosper ('neither side gave way'), Cassiodorus, Hydatius ('not far from Metz', 300,000 dead), Isidore, the Gallic chronicle of 511 ('at Troyes, at the place Mauriacus'), the Copenhagen continuation ('at the fifth milestone from Troyes'), and Gregory of Tours with the vision in Saint Peter's and Aetius' trick.

Italy in 452: Aquileia and the storks, Pope Leo on the Mincio (Jordanes; Prosper, who blames Aetius; Hydatius, who credits famine and an army from the East). Jordanes' second war in Gaul and Thorismud killed by his brothers. Attila's death after Priscus: Ildico, the funeral song, the three coffins; and Marcellinus: 'stabbed by the hand and knife of a woman'. The Nedao. Aetius murdered by the emperor in 454: 'with him fell the Western realm'. Then the afterlife: Gibbon's 'last victory … in the name of the Western empire', Creasy's 'Germanic element', the Kaiser at Bremerhaven in 1900 and Kipling's 'The Hun is at the gate!' (1914).

missing.warum: The usual English Jordanes is not used: Charles C. Mierow died in 1961, and his translation is not yet public domain in Germany. Jordanes is translated here from Mommsen's Latin, with Hodgkin's free English extract of 1892 where it serves.
missing.quelle: Mierow, The Gothic History of Jordanes (Princeton 1915)

missing.warum: Bury (1923) and Hodgkin (1892) translate most of the embassy; the shorter fragments on Honoria and on Attila's death are translated here from the Greek of Müller and Dindorf.
missing.quelle: Müller, Fragmenta Historicorum Graecorum IV (1851); Dindorf, Historici Graeci Minores I (1870)

missing.kurz: The press version of the 'Hun speech' (1900)
missing.warum: The version of the Kaiser's Bremerhaven speech that compares the troops to 'the Huns under their king Etzel' was printed in the press on 28 July 1900 and gave the speech its name. It is not in the official text, which module 5 carries. It will be added when a scan of a newspaper of 1900 can be checked; modern document collections print it.
missing.quelle: German newspapers of 28 July 1900 (e.g. Weser-Zeitung); German History in Documents and Images (GHI Washington)
